ESSAY Thinking Critically and Analytically about Critical-Analytic Thinking: an Introduction Patricia A

Alexander Published online: 9 October 2014 #Springer Science+Business Media New York 2014 In October 2013, 18 scholars from such varied disciplines as educational policy and leadership, cognitive neuroscience, developmental psychology, language and literacy, social psychology,measurement and assessment, and educational psychology gathered together for 2 days ofintense and informative discussion and debate

The catalyst for this gathering was a grant fromthe American Educational Research Association ’s Education Research Conferences Program, awarded to Alexander, Wentzel, and Dunbar, intended to stimulate interdisciplinary discoursearound complex and significant educational issues with the goal of promoting researchinitiatives and sparking reform in policy and practice

In keeping with that laudable intention, the goal of this specific assembly of multidisciplinary scholars was to tackle one of the more salient and recurring themes in contemporary educational theory and practice: What does itmean to think critically and analytically and how can critical-analytic thinking be measuredand fostered in our children and youth

The purpose of this special issue on critical-analytic thinking is to share conundrums, insights, and recommendations that arose from this multidisciplinary assembly and thesubsequent examinations that have arisen from the continuing conversations among theattending scholars with the broader edu cational psychology community
The cross- disciplinary contributions that form this special issue deal with such core topics as the nature,development, assessment, and training of critical-analytic thinking

Those who have contrib-uted to this conference and this issue feel strongly that these scholarly treatises can prove invaluable for those already invested in or concerned with this foundational subject, as well as those seeking to better understand what critical-analytic thinking is, why it matters, and how itcan be measured or shaped

There is no question that changing standards for curriculum, as evidenced in the Common Core State Standards (CCSS; National Governors Association Center for Best Practices andCouncil of Chief State School Officers 2010), now having been adopted by 48 states, and the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS Lead States 2013), seeking to transform science practices, have put the construct of critical-analytic thinking in the forefront

There is no definitive definition of critical-analytic thinking that shapes currentpolicies and practices and no highly regarded or widely accepted measure of critical-analyticthinking that exists within the field —at least not yet

In effect, although such significant curricular and assessment initiatives as CCSS or PARC speak clearly and directly to the need for school-aged populations to engage in critical-analyticthinking, there appears to be little in the way of consensus or certainly within the extantliterature regarding critical-analytic thinking ’s nature and the course of its development
Likewise, there are serious concerns as to how the individual differences that humans manifestmay alter the process and outcomes associated with critical-analytic thinking

Further, there aresignificant issues pertaining to how this elusive construct can be and should be reliably and validly assessed or what techniques or approaches work best to promote critical-thinking in children and youth —both in and out of school

Thus, this special issue serves an important and timely purpose for the educational research community and for those in positions of educa-tional leadership who are charged with the improvement of the educational experience for alllearners

Critical-Analytic Thinking One long-held belief shared by educational researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and the general populace is that schools and society benefit when individuals or groups are perceptive and attentive to the world around them and manifest the ability to think deeply and flexibly about important issues, that is, when they think critically and analytically (e.g., Dewey 1933; Bloom 1956; Halpern 2001;Ku 2009)
The very foundation of a democratic society is a citizenry capable of and willing to engage in such critical-analytic thought (Westheimer 2008)
Moreover, education within democratic societies is presumed to contribute to the developmentof such a thinking and reasoning populace

However, there is ample evidence that this laudablegoal is unrealized for many citizens of the USA and that far too many students lack theknowledge, beliefs, skills, and strategies required to think critically and analytically (Arum andRoksa 2011)

Although investment in the study of critical-analytic thinking has waxed and waned over the past century, there is currently a heightened interest in this higher-order mode of thought, as well as an increased concern as to how to promote it in students of all ages, backgrounds, and abilities (Schraw and Robinson 2012)

There are many reasons that interest in critical-analytic thinking has moved to the forefront in the scholarly discourse, and its investigation has beenapproached from a variety of theoretical and methodological perspectives

Common Ground Claims and Model With this general framing as backdrop, the scholars in attendance at the invita- tional conference, “Se ek in gC om mo nG rou nd , ”set out to engage in critical- analytic thinking about critical-analytic thinking

Based on their empirical and theoretical knowledge rooted in varied dis ciplines, these scholars participated in rich discussions and rigorous debate —posing arguments and counterarguments supported by competing perspectives and research traditions

Yet, as a collective,they shared the espoused goal of not only solely sharpening the differences that existed among them but also of striving for consilience, a term introduced byWhewell ( 1840 ) and used by Wilson ( 1998 ) to describe unity of knowledge across varied disciplines

For the proposers of this conference ( Alexander, Wentzel, and Dunbar), this consilience would hopefully take the form of shared claims about critical-analyticthinking that crossed philosophical, psyc hological, and methodological lines and that could guide future research and instruc tional practice in the years to come

The conference organizers did not intend that th ere be complete or unwavering agreement from contributing scholars since such outcomes are rarely realized in interdisciplinary examinations of complex constructs
But, they did hope for strong cross-disciplinary statements that could be shared with others
Indeed, this hoped-for goal was realizedin the form of the Shared claims that appear in Table 1
